sorry for you. I am sorry for you. I am sorry for you.”

The prince did not recognize the amusing tone and question behind
the expression of tenderness and almost intimacy. He wondered whether
it was not the Empress’ voice, and whether he could only hear a
skilful imitation. He inquired, in a somewhat different tone, “Is the
Empress receiving her niece and nephew?”

“Her Majesty is very much pleased with the young people,” answered
Anna Pávlovna. “They call her the Duchess and the Younger. But this
is not my opinion, but the opinion of Her Majesty’s dear sister,
naïve and not quite so enlightened as herself. Do you know that
Brienneur will fall on the stones?”

The prince did not see her point.

“There are only a few men who will remain on this side of the
Alps,” said Anna Pávlovna. “And that is no more than can be expected
of a man of the world, who, as you know, is more of an idealist than a
realist. And how will the Emperor retain many of his generals? He will
at the very least lose three or four of them, like Suvorov and Kellermann
at the battle of Austerlitz, because they will fear that they may be
immediately called to account. With the exception of two or three men
of such genius that they will never be called to account, the rest
will soon feel in the hands of the Emperor and his wife and daughters the
tyranny of a prince. I hope the young people are not aware that many
great men are being murdered, and that they, too, may be murdered...”

She was interrupted by the entrance of the two visitors. “Monsieur,”
said the prince, turning to the senator, who was ushered into the room.
Then turning to the Abbé Morio, he said, “What brings you to the capital
to-night, Monsieur?”

“Pray excuse me,” replied the Abbé Morio, “dear madame, I cannot be
audacious enough to tell you.”

“I see,” replied the Prince, who had formed an opinion on the
abbé’s character before he entered.

“Have you heard of the assassination at the house of the journalist
Léon Beauval? Did Wintzingerode receive any information?”

“Yes, sir, he received a letter from Baron Necker, telling him to
preserve his safety and that of his brother, the adventurer. He did so,
though he may have been much too cautious (I consider this man
impolitic)....”

“That’s what I feared, Monsieur. Do you know that de Massel has been
assassinated?”

“Not yet, sir.”

“Assassinated! You don’t know?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Don’t be afraid. Had he been murdered, you would have known about
it before you arrived.”

“Monsieur, I fear for you, perhaps in return.”

“Do you know that the assassins have escaped?”

“Not yet, sir.”

“Don’t be afraid. This morning at ten o’clock Madame Marie Antoinette
received a message from a woman who wanted to be heard and was put in
the bed she occupies in the second room. She had been summoned by the
Emperor’s wife and has been informed of her husband’s death.”

“May I ask for what reason?”

“Of course she was not satisfied with this answer.”

“I see,” said the Prince, becoming silent, and then lighted on a
piece of paper. “The Emperor has become a widower and has a daughter
to sustain him. That is all that we know!”

“May I ask—why has the Empress not been told about the assassination
of her brother?”

“His lordship is not at home at the time, sir,” replied the prince.
“Monsieur, the Emperor’s wife has been told of the assassination.”

“Is the Empress here?”

“She is now at St. Petersburg and will come here on the 16th,”
said the capricious Madame de Wintzingerode.

“Is the Empress sick?”

“Very much so.”

“Why?”

“It would be useless to detail all her sorrows.”

“May I ask—what of your brother?”

“Monsieur, my brother did not leave his house. We do not know where he
is.”

“Where are you?”

“In St. Petersburg.”

“Monsieur, you have a wife,” continued Anna Pávlovna, who had
joined the conversation. She was not the only one who did not
feel like it. “Where is she?”

“She is not there,” replied the prince. “She is at her residence at
Smolny. I know that, since her brother died, she has been very much
sick. She is the humblest of servants.”

“And this,” continued Anna Pávlovna, “does not become the wife of a
prince.”

The prince did not see the irony in the remark, but he became serious.
Thank God, Anna Pávlovna believed in the nobility of her family.
She had long been a woman of the world, she had diversified her
relations, and she was not only rich but in high standing.

The abbé Morio arose and bowed to the prince. Then he bowed to Anna
Pávlovna and bowed again and lightly touched each in turn the two
princesses and they bowed to him.

“I thank you for your kindness, and I shall see you again,” said the
abbé, as he turned to exit, and added as he left, “I am at your service
if you are sick.”

Anna Pávlovna had also bowing at the abbé and then turning to the
prince, “Come, then,” said she, “you are not afraid to put in a
appearance at my fete. What have you heard about it?”

“Nothing,” replied the prince. “Though there is no fete.”

“For how long?”

“No longer than yesterday. It is almost over and the whole
government has gone to the country. I have heard that the ambassador
is safe too.”

“Come, then,” said Anna Pávlovna, and the two friends walked out into
the garden.

The prince followed her, but she did not turn her face towards him.
Meanwhile, however, the abbé had been listening with interest,
transfers of fortune were at a loss to him. Anna Pávlovna’s sudden
intensity and her attitude of repulsion to the abbé made slight
influence on him.

The two friends walked in the garden, to which Anna Pávlovna had
attached great importance, for it was a receptacle of all that was
glorious, and contained all that was beautiful and glorious in
St. Petersburg at this time. In her garden she had placed the
precious vine of her charming nature, and finding it there, the prince
allowed something of his reserved nature to show itself.

“Today, there was a Mme. Balland who did not know that her
visit was on a visitation,” said he, and he was clearly amused by the
poise and grace of the young princess, who had just lost her mother. “I
did not know she was coming.”

“Ah, she is a noblewoman who is well-educated and has a wonderful
mind,” replied Anna Pávlovna. “She has thought of the future, of the
future reign, and she wants to make a name for herself. She says she
wishes to be called a princess, and the Emperor confirms her
desire. The princesses of this country have, of course, still a good
deal to learn.”

“I’ve heard of her,” said the prince, “not to mention having met one
and another of the princesses.”

“Oh, come, tell me!”

“But I don’t know Mme. Balland,” said the prince, somewhat
disconcerted.

“I am sure you do. You know her very well,” replied Anna Pávlovna in
a tone of reproach and remonstrance.

“It’s a pity that you haven’t known her better, for she is an
excellent woman, and I do not know if there is a more happy wife for
an emperor. Anyway, my dear Annette, you have never really known me.
You know me only in a courtly way. Women do not know me very well,
though they have heard that I am a great talker. They have heard
that I am a good speechmaker. I’m not like Mme. Sèvres,” said the
prince, whose tone betrayed a sense of conscious inequality. “I am
always silent, and I hardly ever speak except in a courtly way.”

“Ah, what a lovely little phrase,” said Anna Pávlovna, who had
thoroughly enjoyed the contrast, “but I am not so ill-educated
as that woman,” she added in a tone of derision. “What a
delightful woman she is! She is very reserved in her manners. I have
never noticed her bottomless pockets, but I have heard that they are
very numerous. I have heard that she is a very good woman, and that
she loves her husband. This brings me to the subject of my tour. I
do believe that there is a greyhound about the Empress’ house. Is
there?”

“Excuse me, Madam,” replied the prince, slightly taken aback by the
question, “I have never heard of such a thing.”

“Ah, come, be discreet,” said Anna Pávlovna. “It is a fact,” she
added. “Tell me how it is with you, then. There isn’t a man in
St. Petersburg that you don’t like.”

“The question has been put to me by some of my friends,” replied
the prince. “And you are quite right. Of course, the Emperor is my
grandfather is my most beloved person. He is always kind to me. But
if you want to know about me, I have had no chance to meet a single
stranger, and,” continued the prince with some vexation, “I never
take delight in talking.”

“That is most natural, my dear prince,” said Anna Pávlovna, who
had taken a liking to the prince and was pleased to find that he was
not a party to the general gossip. “I have often said it,” she added,
“that the Emperor’s wife and her sister, Madame Marie Antoinette, are
neither the best nor the worst of women. Though her husband has been
abandoned by her, and she has remained in the House of Assembly, she
is a good woman and not a woman to be castigated.”

But, as the conversation went on, Anna Pávlovna became indifferent
to the prince. She was talking to Morio about the Duke of Choveskoy.
She had not heard of his assassination and had not mentioned it. She
was thinking of Anatole. She had lost her son, and her son’s child.
Too much imagination had been allowed in the conversation, and it
seemed as if the prince was speaking of Anatole and Anatole was
replied to by the prince. Anna Pávlovna was looking at him. She
was evidently amused at his sudden change of nature.

“Prince,” she said, “I’ve heard that you have a manner of your own.
It’s very charming.”

“Have a little patience, then,” replied the prince. “I’ve not got a
manner at all. I’m very shy and garrulous. I’ve not got the manners of
common people, but I do not care for them.”

“Then you are not a prince at all?” said Anna Pávlovna, as if the
prince were indeed a commoner.

“Not at all, madame,” replied the prince in a tone of acquiescence.

With these words she bent her eyes towards the prince, as if in
conversation and with certitude of soul, but in a tone of implacable
coldness.

“Am I the luckiest man in the world?” said Prince Vasíli with a
smile.

“I hope, and frequently say, that you will have luck to find and have
more children.”

Her eyes still followed the prince’s lips.

“Not many,” he observed politely, “but I meant, in this case, I meant
at the moment, in my heart.”

“Pardon me,” he added bitterly. “If I had a son in the army, or in a
naval battle, or in the Crimea, I should wish him dead to save the
feudal system. But I had Anatole, and I must be happy.”

“More sons you have, then?” continued the woman.

“Two,” replied the prince, without looking at her.

“Three,” he paused and added, “four. Indeed I want a son in the army,
in the Navy or in the Crimea, but I know that my wife will not permit
me.”

“My dear prince, have you never seen me?” said Anna Pávlovna, with
tears in her eyes.

“No, I haven’t; I am afraid of, and, I am not well.”

“Still, don’t you wonder, that this skin you have don’t call you
Maurice?”

“Now then, Anna Pávlovna, listen to me. I understand that you wish
to say the words. Do you wish to have a son in the army, or in the
Naval fleet, or in the Crimea, but why, dear lady, my wife refuses to
permit me.”

“I don’t like him,” she broke in, interrupting him. “And you know
why he is not with you, in spite of all your efforts? Listen!” and
she repeated her title, with emphasis.

“Prince Vasíli, I am on my death bed, and I wish you farewell,”
he said, and all his eyes shone with anguished anxiety.

Anna Pávlovna raised her eyes and her eyelashes with a heartless
smile.

“Anatole? No, never,” said Prince Vasíli, who did not wish this
unpleasant interview to go on so long and followed her by a short
silence. “But never see me before I die? Never?”

She turned to him without smiling, but her eyes were full of
compassion.

“Never, now or forever. In the event of my death, I will be with you
on your death bed,” she added in a soft voice.

Prince Vasíli pretended to be completely disconcerted by this
affectionate, even maternal, surprise, and Anna Pávlovna could not
help herself. She bent her head towards Prince Vasíli’s eyes, and
she had only just done so when she heard a noise as of a door opening,
and then she saw the shadow of a man entering the room through
the doorway.

Venerable wrinkles had begun to show on the old lady’s face. She
brought her hands together, her eyes rolled, and her nostrils with
all grace, gave play to each other.

“Moi!” cried the old woman, to whom the incident seemed to have
some explanation. “The truth! the truth! Is it true? I saw you in the
living room,” she added, with a smile, the smile of a woman who had
heard her wished name many times. “And I told you that you would be
happy. I told you that you would marry, and that you would have a
son, a son in the army, or in the Navy, or in the Crimea. And so you
married, and you left me, but I didn’t know if you would have a son
and I didn’t know if you would be happy. I knew too that you had been
plagued by that horrid symptom, and that you had allowed your wife to
do her duties. I couldn’t understand why you didn’t remain with me,
too. And now you have left me. What can I do you? What can I ask of
you? You don’t have any money. I have only three hundred roubles. I
have had only one of your poor wives since I married you. You are a
kind man. But I have been a poor woman, and now I am poor, poor, and
poor. It was very kind of you to come and stay with me. I haven’t a
bedroom. I haven’t a bedroom. I have only a bedroom. I have a room
without a bed. I have only a room without a bed. I have no child!
Pray, my dear Prince, when you have seen the handwriting on the wall,
and know that you don’t have a son, and if, like the old woman who
stayed with me, you don’t have a bed, comfort yourself with a bed. I
have a bed. But now I am dead. I am dead. I will be dead. My poor
son, Anatole, my son Anatole, is dead. Let me go to him. Oh, let me
go to him.”

The old woman threw herself down on the sofa, turned her head towards
the prince, whose eyes were full of compassion.

prince’s hand away, and held it to her lips, as if to sink it into her
skin. “There is a word of farewell, a last word, a last wish. Thank
you for having shown me that there is a son. Although your wife is

of your poor wives in return for your kindness. I have a bed. But I

Anatole, is dead. I don’t know where he is. I have heard that he is
wandering in Europe, but he is wandering in Europe. I don’t know if he
is coming back. So I must take a journey to make him. And I shall take
a journey into England. I have heard that you are rich. You have a
son. I don’t know if you have a son. You have a son. I want to see him.

me the favor. Do me the favor. Do me the favor.”

The old woman’s hands lay in her lap, in a pitiable fashion, she was
blind and I could not see how she had done it, what she had done. Her
eyes, however, shone as if they had been filled with tears.

He knew no more how to comfort her than I knew how to console a
child. He had been comforted since childhood by the feeling of
maternal love. He had seen girls’ and young women’s faces covered with
tears, and he had spent hours comforting them for a few minutes. He was
often mistaken for a woman and his house was full of young women, women
in mourning. He had a wife who was always clad in a black gown, nor
had he had time to be more refined than his sister, who died young,
and a daughter Anatole married to the last friend of her father, who
could neither have a fountain nor a rose. But he had never found a
man who could console a woman, the poor one, in such a way, that she
would have said: “Try harder.”

Anna Pávlovna, however, was not very angry with this unexpected
interruption.

“A little while,” she said, in a tone that distinctively belonged to
her, “and now, my dear prince, how come you to have a curious and
tongue without which you talk so much?”

She nodded to the princess and concluded her interview in the most
amiable and most amiable manner.

But the prince realized the meaning of her words, and did not understand
them.

Anna Pávlovna, seeing the embarrassment in his face, and his
discomfiture, and not knowing how to help him, again turned towards
the old woman.

“Madame, what have you to say to me?” she asked, and she stole
together her eyes to his, which he had never done.

But she was not replying to him, but to her own mind. Every
moment, in a hasty conclusion, in a short phrase, she would have
said or done something very odd, one of those strange things that she
said or did without thinking. Now she was proposing to him a wide
range of topics, and she did not understand this, but she understood
it, and her eyes still followed his. And Anna Pávlovna, who had a
great deal to do, was one of those conversationalists who have an
unlimited range of subjects at their disposal. Her fume of emotion is
always at hand, and she calls out its name. She does not tire of it,
not even when she has gone far from the subject. Keeping her eyes
fixed on the prince, she went on by the way of the old woman, and
the prince, without understanding what she was doing, did not answer
her, and his eyes followed hers. In the end, having exhausted the
subject, he got up and bowed, and then still without knowing what
she meant, she rose also, and, with a smile, camouflaged her
discomfiture.

She placed herself on the sofa, her hands resting on her lap, and
she looked around her with a sort of love for everyone.

I myself had gone to see her the day before, and I had not been able
to do so in the following days. I had taken little interest in
Prince Vasíli Kurágin. Anna Pávlovna was no longer the same woman,
but she had become more and more charming. She had lost her beauty, as
well as her feelings, and her mien. Her eyes, her voice, her manner
had become calm and grave, and her easy and attentive politeness was
a man’s fault. She had become more and more refined, and she had
become more and more courtly. She had remained jealous of her
consideration, and always had been more respectful and more civil. She
was no longer the kind of woman who could be manipulated by the hand
of a lover, but she was also far from being the woman who, if she knew
the name of a man, could express her feelings there and then. She was,
as they would say, ‘a woman of the world.’ She had acquired this
martial skill, for she was now a woman of the world, in matters that
interested her. She had acquired that skill, for she was quite a
woman of the world, a woman of the world in this sense, a woman of
the world when she was sick, and she had a sentiment for her patients,
and she was not merely a nurse or an attendant. These were things that
she had learned from experience, and she had made progress, as she
said to me. She had learnt by experience that it was useless to let
on, her smile was never an expression of her feelings. A smile could
not but be the smile of a friend. She had learnt that if you were
a friend you did not smile at the end of a conversation. She had
learned all these from experience. She had learned that in matters
of character, and that sometimes from the hand of a man, or from a
man’s words, the smile could be a sign of a motive, and that she
did not wish to be deceived. She had learned from her husband that
it was better to avoid mentioning her past pleasures, and to talk
on a different subject always, and that she must find a way of
avoiding having to talk on the subject of her husband. She had learnt
all this from her husband, and she had made progress, and she had
made a path for herself, in the sense of ‘a woman of the world.’

And now she had made a path for herself at the court of the Emperor
Alexander. She had got into the house of the Emperor, and, as she
said, she was a woman of the world. She had learned all this by
experience, and she had made progress, and she had made a path for
herself, in the sense of ‘a woman of the world.’ She could not say
more.

“Tell me,” she finally said, as she turned towards the prince, “that
you love me? Do you love me?” She had a gentle, tender face, and she
bent towards him. Her eyes were full of sadness over the death of her
son, and she looked at him seriously. She looked at him as if she
were saying, “If the words you have just spoken are not an imposition,
we shall be married, we shall be very rich, and we shall live well,
and we shall be happy.”

And the prince turned to her, in doubt, perhaps, and seemed ready to
answer.

But Anna Pávlovna, after a few moments’ hesitation, added three more
words, in which she expressed that she had not yet told him the
truth, and that she was sorry.

“Tell me,” she went on, in voice which suggested eloquence, “that
you love me? Do you love me?” She seemed to be saying, “If the words
you have just spoken are not an imposition, we shall be married,
we shall be very rich, and we shall live well, and we shall be
happy.”

And in her last words she threw herself forward on the sofa, and
her eyes shone with emotion.

And the prince, in his turn, turned to her, in doubt, perhaps,
and seemed ready to answer.

quietly: “My dear Anna, if you really love me, I should have the
kind of marriage you have just spoken of, I should be married, and
I should live well and be happy, but I have no sons. I cannot,
and, in the event of my death, I shall be with you on your death bed.

He placed his hand on hers, and she placed her hand on his, and she
depressed her eyes and smiled. His eyes and her eyes seemed to be
quivering with emotion.

tears in her eyes, “that you love me? Do you love me? Do I love you?

“How so, my dear Anna Pávlovna?”

“Why, because you have been married already. You have had a husband.
And yet, since you have had a wife, you have been married. You have had a
wife and you have been married.”

The prince was silent and seemed to be considering. The Princess of
Leningrad had married when she was only twenty years old and had
then been almost as young as her husband. Anna Pávlovna had always
said she had married her husband “in order to get rid of a worthless
one.” She had married him because she was “stupid, and afraid of
being poor,” and because she had “a weak constitution.” She had
married him “because he was handsome enough to make her happy.”
She had married him because she had “a heart that was not big enough
for a husband of her own,” and because she had “a large heart for a
husband who was small.” She had married him because she was “a woman
with no character.” She had married him because she was “very much
infatuated with him.” She had married him because she was “an invalid
and a fool.” She had married him because she was “a woman with more
than her share of good qualities.” She had married him because she
was “an invalid and a fool.”

“Indeed, your heart is very small,” said the prince, seeming to
attempt the same analysis. “Indeed, it is very small as compared with
his.”

Anna Pávlovna, who was not used to seeing her heart treated like
that, seemed to be at a loss, and the prince, observing this, added
in a soft, effusive tone:

“You see I am not the only one who has been deceived.”

“Are you?”


And the prince was silent, and suddenly, without any apparent cause,
he added in his calm, empty tone:

“Don’t you think, Anna Pávlovna, that Madame Chérapin is a
splendid woman? She is a very fine woman, and I am sure she is a
splendid woman.”

“You are not the only one who has been deceived,” said Anna Pávlovna
again, without looking at him, apparently offended by the prince’s
compliments.

“Mademoiselle Chérapin is a very fine woman,” said the prince again,
with a more lively tone, evidently pleased at the compliment, for he
was a man who always gets what he wants. “Give me a few moments.
Certainly, Madame Chérapin is a very fine woman.”

“Prince, you have no right to speak so lightly of Madame Chérapin,
who has been cruelly slandered,” said Anna Pávlovna, so quietly
that it seemed to her that she had just heard her own voice, and he
must be mistaken if he thought he had heard any other. “Madame Chérapin
is an extremely beautiful woman, and she is a very fine woman, a

“Unjustly,” said the prince with a smile, whose eyes were bright and
full of shine.

“Haven’t you ever thought about your three-year-old son?”

The prince bowed and was about to reply, but thought better of it and
said: “His beauty is marred by the accident of his birth.”

“Infamities and horrors,” said Anna Pávlovna, looking reproachfully
at the prince, “so infinite. He is a true child of the revolution.”

“His genius is lost in his mother’s beauty,” said the prince, who
probably made a magnificent figure in a public life. “To disguise a
mother’s beauty one would need a lighted torch. But then, a man with
a torch would be the most radiant. But who hasn’t had a torch? But
who hasn’t had a great mother; as great a mother as a great woman can
be, and a woman in the highest degree! The woman I know best, who is
the woman the greatest and the most beautiful, I can’t name her,
perhaps she is one of those who are called excellent, but aren’t; for
the good, beautiful, and the kind and intelligent are one and
the same—not all the kind and intelligent are good! But the beloved
mother I know—she will make the best child! My dear Vnenia would
show you the picture of her daughter. She will give you more than
you want to see. It is full of love and joy. I will show you the
picture of her unborn child. It will be a masterpiece!”

“I will see it,” said Anna Pávlovna, looking at the prince, who now
showed by his drawn-out smile and closed eyes that he was ready for
anything which did not seem to be serious or unpleasant.

“Once I promised you that I would show you the picture of Anatole. It
will be beautiful, though I have not yet received it. It will be a
masterpiece. It will probably show you a future prince. But I haven’t
yet received the portrait; I expected it, and it was sent away for
its restoration, and it’s not back yet. I was waiting for it. Now, but
I have been called, and I have got to go, that’s all. I wish you
good-bye and hope to see you again soon. Sayonara!”

The prince was again silent, and he took the opportunity to get up and
leave.

and was connected with the Montmorencys. She had heard of him from
Prince Vasíli, and she was familiar with him from her own home. The
former of whom she was much more anxious to meet than the latter,
because she had a belief in the good will of those who had caused her
sufferings and griefs, and who had made her sufferings and griefs worse.
The Abbé Morio was a smiling, radiant, intelligent, and incorruptible
count, who lived on his income, without any extra, and was the first
and only really faithful friend of Anna Pávlovna. She frankly and
without reserve loved him, and about him she wrote to the Empress.

“You don’t realize what a blessing it is to have a lively spirit in
one’s veins. Don’t you think so? You carry yourself too well. We always
represented to you that, health being an asset, your daughter was in
every way inferior to her sister. She has a heart, a spirit, and they
are more by two years. You don’t feel as if she had been born on
earth, or rather, as if she were born in paradise. You did not pretend
so, but you were never too agreeable in her presence and she is
anxious to have you still so. She wants to be your daughter, to keep
your feet firm, and you must give of yourself, and sometimes, my
dear prince. She has supper half an hour later than you, she has very
distinct meals, she goes off to bed she goes for exercise at 9 O’clock,
and if you don’t do those things yourself she will feel obliged to do
them for you. It sounds crude, but she is afraid of the future, and
not only of the future, but of death. I, my dearest, do not understand
her anxiety as if it were not altogether legitimate, so legitimately
motivated. There is an unusual depth of melancholy in your daughter,
she will consider her own existence, rather than usefully consider
the destined fate of her father.”

With these words she looked at her daughter, seeing her walk in
the corridor in the evening, and her face reflected in her candlelight.
Anna stood on tiptoe, watching her, as if she were her. That only
was the beginning. Anna Pávlovna imagined that, if she had been near a
lamp, she herself would have been doing the same, would have seen her
twin’s face, and perhaps, looking into her daughter’s eyes with her
eyes, she would have felt her heart hers.

“Tender mother,” continued the prince, “you have too much taste. They
call you beautiful, but they don’t know how to express all the good
things you have to say or all the good moments you give to your
company. And but for my dear late friend Andreka Skartvy, might I say
she was Carlos’ daughter, the Madame de Beaux-Arts, the composer’s
daughter, there would have been a link with France. I was the only one
who could see and appreciate the true France, the good France. I was
the only one who saw through the Fascists. Feel yourself better. You
will be better, Anna. I am sure of it. And it will be to your credit
being patient with those whom you don’t understand,” she added, with a
fond glance at the prince’s brow beneath whom she was a person of the
highest nobility and reputation and renown.

Since her father had been compelled to recede from the cause of the
emigrant party, since 1805, Anna Pávlovna Schérer had become the
natural heir to the name and character of the Maréchal Gladievsky and
her brother, son of that famous officer, Prince Theodore Dubotsky.
From the middle of January of the present year, when the emigrant
party, after a long succession of sharp struggles and raids and
stretches and defeats, had finally reserved destiny and been permitted
to obtain before the revolution an existence of liberty and honor,
until that date her brother is known to have been passive, incapable of
rebellion. However, his brother, Prince Alfred, is called the
‘Battleaxe,’ the Revolutionary Commander, and the spokesman of all.
Just as her brother has not been able to support the party in matters
of war, so she has been able to support it only in the dilemmas of
the French Revolution.

Anna Pávlovna Schérer had only survived as Countess von Plénovie and
Marquise Plénovie, but her daughter, Vyshinsky, is a new existence,
but one which she has had to consider, with Verdialilité, through all
the revolutions, and as the successor of the hereditary dukedom of
Lucca and Genoa upon the death of her ancestress, Madame Plénovie.

Anatole de Vyshinsky was the son of Vyshinsky and Rebecca Krakhóva.
He was a son of the only famous regicide, the last of the house,
October, 1805. The arch-heretic, Alexey Andréievitch, had settled
after the first of the revolutions at the domain of Vyshinsky. He
continued there till the death of his wife. He continued also the
family of souls at Vyshinsky’s, until the death of the naive and
beautiful Anastasia, the last wife of the grandfather of the present
equerry. The Counts Bleidschütz lived in the house. So did the son of
the concierge of the Porche. So did their delicately grown-up son,
Gorbovsky. Their only daughter, historian, painter, poet, entertainer,
has remained with them till death. There, too, lies the Countess
Yurievna, who was Princess Yarévna de Plénovie. The maiden aunt of
the Russian court, in whose house her grandfather Krakhóv lived till
his death. He had just given her a beautiful annuity. He had a very
honest wife, who has brought him by succession into the world Kshesiv.
The Admiral, and this man has been a Cologne consul. Chief of
counsellors and Grand Vizier at St. Petersburg, the son of Ghering.
The Prince of Verona, the Prince of Russev. And lastly, the niece of
Count Bleidschütz, Maximiliane de Plénovie. An annuity, with
property, and with a beautiful young woman at the hands of whom he
had been indulgently lifted from St. Petersburg, the place of tiring
affairs, to St. Petersburg the place of gaieties. She has been a
very good field-marshall, but there are things in her that are
very bad. It is General décéré, with the old style of a man in the
lines of Napoleon’s war, a Mostel-bird of St. Petersburg and of
all Russia’s war-dept corps.
Her another cousin, the favorite of the Empress Fëdorovna, the Empress
Mariana Fëdorovna. But she remains very faithful in her secret
affections to her own country and her own reign. As soon as she is
elected Queen of the Romanov Dynasty, Anna Pávlovna Schérer will
see that she aspires to be known as the Emperor’s Valera-Pastréna,
the Queen of the Romans. She has a grand recent wealth at her
expense. She will have a fine residence in Prague. On the other
hand she will be an ally of the Empress Matthias, the émigré
Prince-Bishop Lannyns, and her brother Prince Andrek is her brother
and will remain very important. She is very intelligent and
enchantresses the epigones. But she is in reality a round, proverbial
woman and a woman whose sex is of the highest benefit to the court
and the Empire.






CHAPTER XII

In the course of the afternoon Anna Pávlovna remained only half
an hour at home, and she was disconsolate and impatient to go to
find out her sister’s fate. But she continued her conversation with
Prince Vasíli Kurágin and asked him questions. He did nothing
but screw his brows and with that expression of disappointment and
alas! that he often assumed when he had to answer questions, or else
when he did not know the answer. She said to him, as if she had only
noticeably remarked these questions, persistently: “And about his
Consulate. Can anything be more horrifying than the Consulate? What
useful thing can that be to a country?”

“Do you think so?” said he, fixing his eyes on Anna Pávlovna and
shrugging his shoulders. She had given him, with annoyance and
impetuosity, her own intentions, her ideas and her ideas concerning
events and a world. She thought to myself that she must be obeyed and
was enraged at him for his slow, almost mercantile manner.

Therefore, she said quickly: “I am only waiting for the order,
then I will go into the street. I have such a horrible feeling.”

“Then go,” answered the prince, who had risen as she said this. With
the elegance peculiar to Prince Vasíli Kurágin, he raised the elbow
on which he was sitting and put his shoes on the cushion without
fluffing the spatterdashes, covering his ankles under the pantaloons.
“It is better that you do not wait for the order of the president of
the Directory. It is better that you should go and see me, for that
has just been done.”

“Aren’t you annoyed at wishing to join the Russians?” she queried,
looking at him, but laughed. He assumed the habitual attitude of a
courtier and of a bored courtier. She put her hat upon her head. He
did the same. Then he seated himself on the sofa beside her again
and they began to converse upon domestic subjects.

“Why don’t you go to Vyssoli?” said Anna, who had made this remark
with that keener and favored suggestion to Prince Vasíli Kurágin,
which the prince was not likely to reject and which she was so
encouraging. “And the Court? What say the Court?”

“Well, everybody is of the same opinion,” said he, “that it is better
to stay at home.” He thought for a moment, then answered: “Well, but
did I not send Forjákov to Paris?” and the prince immediately
continued: “He would have said no, but he didn’t find it out. I
made the doctor tell me that I must go to Astolph.”

“Astolph?” she repeated, with a sigh, as if she had heard it for
the thousandth time. She showed that she was tired of reading it and
that she wanted to leave it. She leaned over the sill and gave him a
full view of her beautiful young face, her shining and laughing eyes.
“You haven’t heard it? In France there will be a president of the
Republic and a Senate who is really representative of them and not
servile.”

“He is our Dimitry Fëdorovitch,” said the prince carefully,
proceeding to the succession: “To accept so fine a prize, to humiliate
the arch-Bourbon and to make bad France valuable to Napoleon is all
very magnificent. But what do Napoleon foresee for next year? The
prize, but it will not be an immense prize. His success is over.
Education is over; France has hardly even begun to originate the
priceless idea, and it will remain a waste paper of forgetting. It must
be done separately. Europe must reunite.” He was tired again.

“Shall I see the Cardinal?” she asked, consoling him, and smiling.

“Don’t get upset dear,” he said, “I was only teasing you. It is not
a great cost for the household to send a carriage, especially as all
around Paris are going the same way.”

“That is it. Let us send it.” He looked at her, and he was filled
with the utmost soberness.

“I know they do not come,” he added, sighing greatly, “but that one
thinks one,” and he approached the subject, which he had not
without difficulty avoided.

“Shall I write a letter to Father Grant, the Secretary of the
College of Science, and to his assistant von Thaanni, asking them to
occupy their time with the prospects of Science?”

Anna Pávlovna smiled, laughing, but she was so concerned that she
said: “If I don’t do this, I shall shudder. My father is very
instructed and he has splendid faculties. Was Sévigné much more
instructed than Voltaire? Did he not write brilliant works? But how
single-minded he was. All his genius did not bring him the sweet
wages and he became envious of amiable Terese whose genius was less
exultant. What was Voltaire’s dream? Let us hope,” she added, and the
levity of her smile deceived him for a moment; he almost turned his
head, taking his pen off the paper, then he continued, almost in
a whisper: “Do you know that there has been in some Native American
cosmopolis an expedition sent by a French admiral to the spot
where ^Anna-elê-nie^ is supposed to have washed her hair?”

Anna Pávlovna spake up with an effect and with the same sentence,
She almost concluded her sentence. Forsome improvident words had
jammed her tongue, and she could not, by the breakwaters offered to
her tongue, break out, and she did the effect of the words, which she
could not break out, and she lost time. Poor woman, she, an
inexhaustible brain and a mind greater than that of her distinguished
brother, could not find an answer to this speech. Therefore she
gave him the impression that she had confused herself with bitter
curses, and that she smiled and made an excuse. She repeated that
she did not know that **Anna-elê-nie** was a historical personage,
but she knew that Napoleon had invented the idea and had made
a fine lump of French prose for his books. Napoleon about ^Anna-Elê-nie^,
and Napoleon about Conservation. Anna stared at him as she said
this word, and he had the embarrassed expression when the reader
cannot get the word.

“I pray you tell me: has there really been in some Native American
cosmopolis, an expedition sent by a French admiral after the battle
of Boulogne-sur-Mer? You may never have heard of it,” she said,
amazed, and the effect of the speech was broken with a hand on her
face.

“But Napoleon,” she said, “there was that for Napoleon. I observe
that he likes Napoleon.”

“I was thinking of a slip from thinking,” said the prince. “What a
sweet thing! Indeed this hemisphere, this illustrious Neptune,
**Vassal-nin-de-l’immel**, if we must call him, probably takes that
fancy in all things. Does he want us to get a more perfect
objectification of mankind? I wonder,” he asked, with design, after
a quick glance at Anna’s expression, which was full of _diversité_ ;
“I wonder what Napoleon would have been if he had been sent to
Crete to turn it into a republic? And if he had been attached to
France by a chain of meteorological rays, of which he would have
instantaneously smelt the family of Napoleon and the family of
Voltaire and thought he would have nothing to do with them? And if
he had had that pastime and could mathematically foresee the
movements of your three great boys, your **Lemnæsties, the Peau-de-peau
Napoleons, and the Napoleon-(E), the Napoleon-Colonels**? He would
have done like a hero, like an **Albie-en-ambitie', completed
by the touch of the illustrious French character. He would have
done like Prosper Albie-en-ambitie à la mode de Voltaire. He would
have had a heart like yours: what a heart! He would have had
a lively spirit like that of your Lateinae, so wild and so
uncontrolled, he would have had a clear intelligence and a caustic
sense of humor like ^Elé-no-ble*’. And then, how, in your bondage,
how, in your prison of the Revolution, the dissolved and all-penetrating
spirit of Voltaire’s genius, so pure, so sparkling, how in your
bounden country, how in your republic, is that dead, timid Napoleon
ever going to rise to its proper eminence? I am going on like
dramatic script-writing. I will name everyone in Paris, in all
Ireland.”

“Yes, Napoleon, his genius is a Paris genius,” she added, half
sincerely, but she wanted to express her approval of a thesis so
original. She listened for a moment to the prince’s words and her
expression again ceased. She leaned forward again, with the exact
correspondence of the French word, and the expression of a woman
who is ready. The prince said hardly and without emotion: “So? How do
you feed yourselves in Paris?”

“And in Ireland?” she said, with a smile and criminally wanting
her left eye. But she said that more diplomatically, in a manner in
which a condemned woman with heart and soul calls for help.

Anna P. smiled and regretted her having lost her choker, but she
showed no other expression. She fixed her eyes on the prince’s
face and kept her private conversation with him.

“Nothing, to search for a stucco,” said he; “we eat bread, cheese,
like others. We eat lamb and if we are on the coast we eat fish and
sea-duck. But besides, we share with the French and the Irish the
grace of having fish, eggs, and wild chicken for our breakfast; we
even eat cheese. If we are Frenchmen, it will not be the same. But if
we are also Irishmen, it will be the same. However, we only very
partially. We only eat three months here of other food.”

He finished with an air of pleasure. She gave an expression of
dissatisfaction. She wanted him to tell her about his triumphs.

“And you?” she asked after a pause, at the end of which she had
said to herself that she desired revenge. He began slowly, he said
he was very cheerful, very dissatisfied, and he seemed not to
understand what a _malaise_ he had. She could not continue their
conversation. She wanted to draw him away; she wanted to hear of the
Revolution, of the fighting, of the treason, of the triumphs and
repellents. A man goes to the circus; a woman goes to the
pavilions. He said, and his Irish laced himself into her soul, like
in Ireland, where only the best have left Ireland. He said, and
her heart was full of them. He said, and in order that she might
not pass him by she said over and over again: “The victory of the
people in Genoa, the victory of the Church in Vienna, the French
regicide, the duel of Perec; Odette’s retreat; the Frenchmen’s
‘retraite’, and the ‘retreat’ at Prague. Well, I don’t understand,
but I feel,” and she left off her words. She could not recover herself
with him; she and he were in a different world. She went to find
Anna on her arrival. He followed her.

Anna watched her daughter, and she saw her at the hostess’s residence.
Anna quietly followed, and she did not see her because she had not
dreamed that she was there. She knew something of the Grand Vicomte,
but nothing of him, and she was astonished by Anna’s justice; she
was going to see the Countess de Moria. She had not seen her since
the revolutions. She did not know if she was there when she had
heard that she was called. Strangely enough, she went there. She was
surprised by the sight of the Grand Vicomte; but that said little,
not even a genealogical question had been settled. Anna followed her,
it was clear that she did not know Anna, but that Anna was a person
of kind hospitality, without reserve and with a wide knowledge of
things. She had not seen her, because she had not known her; but they
became friends, and Anna knew now, and Anna understood. Most
important, Anna Pávlovna understood, and the Major went with it.
The good and accomplished Grand Vicomte had, under that title,
opened a new path to Anna Pávlovna. He had quietly taken her into
his protection, and he had also taken the confusion she wore him
into, just as he had not chosen to see him; but he and she were now
in a closer intimacy.

### **CHAPTER XIII.**

The Grand-Curé, Regency, Minister of Education, Grand-Souspré, and
The Recruiting Mayor

Of all the columns in the peninsula renowned only for being the
best living room and enjoyable, intelligent and alive and the best
residence of that most modern and gentlemanly of entertainers, the
Baron de La Gloixy has especially been held the best living room;
but of all the great rooms in the thick wardrobe, of which there
are plenty, and with which there is an overwhelming diversity of
color and etiquette, there is the best living room occupied by
a man of several times, so that he can think, respond to, refute and
join in all the things that pass in the living room, as if it
were one’s own personal right to the richest position within the
living room, a position which best serves one’s spirit and mind,
that illustrious man and adherent of the Emperor Alexander, whose
name is maître d’hoste de guéguerourinz, which is the
equivalent of maître d’escalope.

“Failure, failure, failure,” he said, “so much for the
academicians of the Bentotik Palace, the famous versifiers of the
poetry of Alexandre de Duine, thrown by Ignatius on the altar of the
fanaticism of his own clear perception and discarded from that
holy bosom, the greater reward. After this flurry of Remonstrant
commissions and relapses of the Empire, what will be done next? Do
any one think of creating the Academy of Faience under the
supervision of the Grand-Souspré? They will be quite disappointed.
But how will the Academy believe that humanity was not good enough
without making itself good before nature? And without persuasion,
its men who have at the present time and on its future day,
especially those who have at the present time, at least through
the presiding spirit of their valets, the atmosphère for a
considerable future, the being will never become the good man so
comfortable in their own closets? The dreamer that thinks, which
is between those who are good and those who dream: the dreamer that
has not embraced yet some well-known attraction, for the first
time; the dreamer that has adopted the good life in everyday of
life and of mind, and that speaks to himself and is at ease. He is
better than the excellent petit-enfant.”

Indeed, the Grand-Curé has more than once been annoyed by this
adversity of will.

The Grand-Souspré was the member of the Council, the French
counselor, the member of the Council, the king of the Garden,
and grand nephew and guardian of the Emperor Alexander. He was
therefore the coachman of the Grand-Souspré, but he had also
been the coachman of the Grand-Souspré’s uncle, Napoleon Bonaparte.

“Yes, that is true,” replied the prince. “She is very much like
an old cat. I love her to distraction.”

Anatole, who was the time being “whom I appreciate less than
anyone,” stood “at the window.” It was customary at Court in those days,
when a child was born, that the young and beautiful customs of
Masculinity, evoked by the existence of a small brother, was the
vocation of the female elder daughter. Anatole Schérer was born on the
10th of May, 1803, with the latter splendid name and was dressed and
conducted like a male child, attending to affairs of the Court very
much along the same lines as a young man. Such was his natural
ingenuousness that he very soon became the darling of the whole Court,
standing repellently in the midst of the noblesse. Even the noblesse
indulged in envy, for they could not. Anatole was very far from being
one of those nasty little noblesse that gossip made a habit of calling
the Pátines. His devotion, his nice manners, his great sense of
dignity, his intellectual and artistic tastes, his passion for books,
the Duchesse unhappily found him in Paris, where, by his ease in
attending to his studies, he went no less familiarly to the Company of
Bibliophiles. Here he took liberty with men of other tastes, respecting
not even in the slightest degree the Pátines, who were as well as ever
they had been. Here Anatole was a favorite so much for his fine manner
that it was not known that he was not a Pávin. The Duchesse, seeing
him in company with those she had called “pissed,” soon discovered
him; but her curiosity was not satisfied; she had confided her liking
to the Empress, who had received him every day since the Countess of
Baron Montmorency’s birth and had assigned him as the favorite of her
daughter (and she apparently loved Anatole, for during the rest of the
day he was seeking amusement with her). The Duchesse soon found that
she had been happier, more pleasing to herself, more important than she
had any reason at all to be. Anatole had a dazzling brilliancy of
appearance, particularly in his chivalrous courage, and he was never
found without a sword belt, a dagger, or a pistol in his pocket. His
practical conception of womanly simplicity amused his aunt. Anatole
was thrown into the close family circle of the Court; he was
welcomed by the Princess, the Princesses, and even the Duchesse
herself, so that during his first visit he was a favorite even with
the Princess. He shared in all her favor, till one day a heard one—a
much older maiden from the Court and a gentler personage—saying, “In a
few months your daughter will _angel forth_.” To which the Princess
replied, in her dry, natural disposition, “Is not our daughter the
sovereign of Paris?”

Locanto was the sole witness of these facts in Anatole’s favour.
Anatole received him with a cordial hearty welcome, taking care to
consign him to the arms of his charming and expeditious maid of honor.
“And my dear Annette,” he said to her, “have you blamed Anatole for
this youth, who you so readily found at hand when it was necessary,
but who you blame, beyond a shadow of doubt, as not worthy of you?
Tell me right in the name of God what is your opinion.”

Anatole’s subsequent conduct had nothing to disconcert her, for her
inadvertent commencement of the conversation was freely followed by his
apologetic tone. “A nun had the other day called upon me,” he added,
in a very reassured and pleased tone, “because she had been informed
by a supposed friend that you had loved him like a child, and that you
had told him he was like a son. She informed me I had told him what
she had been led to believe. I answered ‘a child?’ and ‘Mr. de
Tol”’s daughter.’ And then she asked me if I had put him out.”

The Princess Satoway smiled. She was admiring him at a much closer
distance; though she told Anatole, “But I did not love you like a
child,” she had done so until now, “for the love I bore was not due
to love but to reason.”

“Then I was a child,” he replied, in a tone of glazed reassurance,
“and a child I had wanted.”

“Wonderful,” said Locanto, who had never seen Anatole before. “How
undeniably a child! And, unheard of! Why, is it in fair France
everywhere to see such a thing?”

“We are splendid,” replied Anatole, smiling, and almost laughing.
“The truth, however, is that if he comes into my old aunt’s hands
he will be a handsome child,” was the reply of the Princess with a
very feline superiority.

When the Princess returned he was useless. He would have fallen had
he been tossed into the street like a box of matches. Since he was
murdered, he had found, to his joyful conviction, that he was even
better in the hands of women than in the hands of men. Anatole was
admired by the girls who were still charming. The Duchesse of St.
Médard, who still remained admirable, called him with many others "a
happy, easy child of the Court," and the Princess, “such a charming
child.” For Anatole, who had made no request at all, festivities, was
a holiday and a time to meet, which explained the very happy manners
He thus obtained a place in the affections of all women that were
gentle—and, finally, a place in the affections of Anatole himself, for
not a day passed but he had Anatole, in the hands of some girl. He was
indeed very fond of the Duchess of St. Médard, but at that time he
had no opportunity to show her his favors. Next day she, however, came
and Anatole went off to her, and made her present with a bouquet of
tulips, which she accepted courteously. He had before handed her
oakumedeine (silk) gloves with a clasped lock, on which was printed a
stone having the Prince’s name and the like of many other things in
gold, never to be worn, as well as a diamond necklace. The Duchess was
very touched and very pleased and so auspicious these gifts, with
her approval Anatole received the tulips in such admirable order that
the countess was also delighted. The Duchesse then played him a trick,
which no one could anticipate. Anatole, who was now a favorite of the
Duchess, and who had thought it a trivial matter to visit her, was
nevertheless astonished to see on her finger a chain of diamonds,
the most extraordinary diamond chain ever seen at Court. An old, quite
grey hairs, uneducated, but apparently heartfelt woman, the Duchess
received and treated him most charmingly, and Anatole had excellent
opportunities of being admired by women of the highest class. Even at
that time he found on numerous occasions their fondness for him.
He was soon elevated and made a favorite of the Princess, the Princess
herself, the Duchess, Madame Chirac, the Empress’s governess, the
Princess of Cartopolská. The dowager Madame d’Esnévalde made an
appreciation of him which was not the same as that of the Princess. The
Princess Schérer, remarkable for her womanly sensibility, listened to
him with greater respect and improved him, as she well knew and was
charmingly grateful for all he did for her; but Madame d’Esnévalde found
in him a real moron, which the Duchesse only admired. Anatole was
celebrated at Court for his charm, his ease, and his propriety, but he
was also something of a rogue. This disparity affected him very much.

He was loved by the Princess, the Duchess, and the Duchess and, in
high society, by the younger daughters of the nobility, to whom he was
born salutary. He thence left behind an innumerable train of
addresses. When he had once approached a lady, he always remained
obscurely happy and pleased; but he was also admitted by them with the
undeniable pleasure he was received. He had the same privileges with
the Princesses that he had with the Duchesses and the Duchesse and
the Princess of St. Médard. Anatole never invited them, but the ladies
came to him. He was with them when they came and he went with them when
they went. Anatole was praised by the noblesse, the ladies of the
noblesse, the ladies of the court, and they admired him most. He was
delighted and charmed by whatever he had not liked, but he lived with
such ease and propriety that though it was known all about him, he was
nevertheless a favorite, and all wished to see him. At this time
he was in the position of being at Court at the Court. But Anatole was
representative of the Court. She was then at her apron-press.

A nephew, at that time a favorite of the Empress, was caused, not without
at first high praise from the Empress, to the astonishment of Anatole,
to be dismissed more than thirteen times, because it was observed
that Anatole had often followed this nephew around the Palace and was at
his beck and call, and because Anatole had admitted an infinitely
reputable child of a famous family to his armpit. The Duchesse very
well knew Anatole and his charms and understood the extraordinary
certainty by which he was adored by all that he represented. At the
same time Anatole impressively gave the Duchesse the knowledge of his
situation, for when she had him at the foot of her throne, she had
the supposed nephew in her lap. The Duchesse, herself a nonentity, was
astonished to find Anatole, as she said, playing with a genuine
popular child like himself, and whose adorations she had
anticipations of in every one that surrounded the Court; but Anatole
answered in a way that she could not understand, and in any case
could not keep up with. Anatole was a favored child, and he pleased
the Duchess, which he did not do in the other Court children. She even
became wounded by him. At this very time Anatole informed the Duchess
herself that she might become the Princess d’Ellemont’s favorite,
that he regarded a daughter of the famous Ger-erogaud more than he had
ever thought of a younger daughter of the Chatillon-Menestrel. Anatole
did not have the least care for them, but he had no intention of
being an uncultivated moll.

On one point, Anatole was to be acknowledged the matchmaker of the
Court, from his youth. Madame Vetch in particular was treated by him
in a most peculiar and highly praised manner. He even discovered the
family secret in view of his aunt, as everything, he said, was in her
hands. Anatole said that the Duchesse had made the Princess d’Ellemont
a present of a diamond necklace, which was startling in reputation
because it was worth 70000 francs. He mentioned that the dowager Madame
had a difficulty with the Princess in not understanding her
practices, but that the Princess of Cartopolská was amused by all such
things. He added that the Princess had been the recipient of the
dowager Madame’s dedicated necklace the preceding year, and had
been much amused by it.

These were only a few of Anatole’s exploits. Without that talent for
which he was famous, Anatole’s humor would have failed him and it is
clearly the case that Anatole’s charm conquered at Court; even the
first ladies of the Court without title to any kind of distinction
admitted Anatole’s virtues, though they were not equal to Anatole’s
to him, for the attraction Anatole had was not one for distinction.
Even in the same Court the similarity of his charm was felt more
deeply than any other quality. Anatole became indifferent to the
atmosphere, to Court life, of which he was unaware. In the midst of
it. noismo his presence was admitted. When he was missed he was not
scarcely found. He was so fair in his humor, so attractive now, that,
though he was friends with almost everyone, his circle was narrow,
which he caused the more. Anatole was, among women and men, a sun
that bore no spot, but covered all with gold. He did not find a
scandal; neither did he seem to be scandalized; he was an angel
without a fault. Anatole was not mite the flower of youth who had
waned, aged, and flattered these persons since his birth; but he was
a child crowned with flowers, who was born into royalty, into the
flower-decked caste of the children of the Court, a war of the
personifications of the Court, who were coveted, loved, chosen by
chosen ones. Anatole was a Diplomat, a perpetual papal secretary.
Anatole was ever the same at Court, as quickly as in Germany, at
Schwerin, in the imperial chamber of Vienna, at the Imperial Castle of
Frankenstein—love him, the most extreme friend of friends, the best
of your friends at any time or place he was. Anatole was the most
favorite of the Court because he was the only one, though hardly
admitted among the noblesse at Court, who was always well affected.
Anatole was not a private child. He made the Court dance like a
church. Anatole was a canon of four Sundays in a year, and a
dame-de-coupes. Anatole enjoyed familiarizing himself with different
classes and he felt the servants in Kirtchgernostheim, a favorite
of the Duchess, as against servants in the Hotel de bouillon, a
favorite of the Princess of St. Médard. In one sense Anatole did
not have a popularity, but he was familiar enough with all his
worshipers; he was not an Occasional Child. He made the Court laugh,
and it listened to him. He amused all the sang-froided members of the
Court and was always listened to. He amused the Prince of Wintzingerode,
the Prince of Kirtchgernostheim, the Baron de Montmorency, the
Prince of St. Médard, and the Baron d’Orbelin. Anatole became
universally popular. Anatole was much beloved by Anatole, Anatole
by Anatole, Anatole by the Duchesse, and Anatole by all the Court.
Anatole was the Prince of Hohenlohe of St. Médard and the Prince of
Clam-Richard. Anatole knew the Dukes of St. Médard better than
anyone. Anatole acted as the envoy of the Duchess to the Court, and
if the Princesses were friendly Anatole desired to become their best
friend, and if the Duchesses were friendly, he had already become
obnoxious to them. Anatole was adored by the Duchennes, the
Princesses, and the countesses of Savoy, Salter (but not by the
Princess of St. Médard), Neckarshrine (but not by the Duchesse de
Clémenceau), and the lily (but not by the Princess). He was the
favorite of the nuns, and of the Alexandrine of the Ger-ernogaud,
and of the Silesian of St. Médard, who, however, in spite of the
identity of her name, was not one of the five daughters of the
Chatillon-Menestrel. Anatole was the boy of the Champollion of the
Saint. Anatole was the Prince of Melbourne and of Rome. Anatole was
not only the Prince of Oldenburg, of the Warburg, and of
Yaïres. At Court he was not even the Prince of London. Even in
the Court his womanly merits and his refined and apparent
moralities were not equivalent to any more than the favorite of the
Court. Indeed, Anatole’s advantages at Court exceeded all possible
comparison, for the Court was brilliant, and so much so that Anatole
was liked and flirted with and he became famous, and attended
Events, and traveled tumultuous episodes, and stood, where Anatole
stood, the partner of noblesse, the family’s favorite of ladies,
the idolized of men, and inspired admiration at Court without
compensation.

Decidedly Anatole was the personification of the feminine Court.
Anatole not only did not laugh the most exactly, but he had never
laughed. Anatole was in fact the favorite of his motherland. All the
women of the Court cast an inmost bewilderment on seeing him for the
first time. The reaction even of the best-appreciated women was almost
unhappiness. Anatole being as perfect as he was, caused Gabrielle
to vex her very much, who, like them, had hitherto had under her
consideration only Anatole’s beauty and had been totally unaware of
his many other charms.

Anatole and Gabrielle were friends, not at all and almost admiring
respect, and for that an opposition, not without love, was felt. Such
an understanding of the friendship of sons and daughters is not very
common, but among friends, above allbred families, it is not rare at
all. Gabrielle, whose sadness was stimulated by the fact that at her
age she should be mothered and at the same time love (as if love
could be easily gained at so great a age), was irritated by Anatole’s
walking about her shadow. See, Anatole was rising up among her, intimates
with her, known to her, yet still regarding her just as dearly as
befitting a favorite. In its turn Gabrielle brought under her
consideration the reality of Anatole’s heart, but this did not
appeal to her, for her very nature had been just as brought under the
consideration of Anatole. Yet these women did not incline to the grimace
of the envy of the most stubborn stone. But a still worse case
occurred.

The prince, regarded without sympathy by a certain degree of
imperturbable luxury, returned hastily to more pleasant reflections.

Anna Pávlovna, who herself was sometimes mistress of social jealousies
and envy, at this moment did not want to discuss personal affairs of
immediate interest and, ignoring the distinction between grand and folk,
or the difference between mere neighbor and noble and rich, she said:

“Speaking of your grand-father, he has just died at Brissier. I was
there myself. He was a good giant, and of noble birth. Was a real mountaineer.
As we say that in this age of print, where printed copies are plentiful,
we print titles, let me print you his grave, and write the address of
our Duchy. In turbas mattresses, as the sole doctors recommend at the
time of death, in a letter from his friends, as a eulogy, and finally
hope him a good Catholic,” hence an evasive reference to his religion.

How was she to advise Prince Vasíli? How much could he stand and who
was fit for him to advice? His country, France, was threatened; his
country, Russia, was constantly deteriorating and lacked heroes. He
had no brother; no cousin; no son could be spared him, nor was he even
a mere decent, practical, congenial, willing and loyal friend. He had
no born general, a choice of which he could be reasonably sure. He had
nothing but his own countries. What was to come troubled him more than
anything else. The most distant ambition of the prince was to become
king like Napoleon, as if it could not be considered shameful or even
appalling that a prince in his hour of greatness, his pride and self-sacrifice
should inaugurate the march to the throne of the
Pyrenees. Such a one would be a symbol of the regal power ([Procris](http://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Procris), a
young king of Paphos, invented by Hercules, to depict pride, falsely
praising his opponent, while he was himself the opponent of his opponent.
[Achilles](http://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Achilles) was a mythical
murderer, the son of Peleus of Phthia, and king of the Achaeans.)
But how could he accomplish this lofty and glorious object? Now that
the flood-waves of revolution and war were issuing from the Atlantic
beaches, how would his nobility respond to the insurrection and how
would his heart respond to revolution? Should he not deprive himself
of all worldly interest and attain it through one of himself? But as
nothing and no one could endure what is happening and as if the
oppressive hand of the Austrian and French troops had been touching
his heart and soul, he was preparing to put an end to this present
depression of the heart and soul and nobility by becoming king.

The prince answered the question without extraneous ornamentation and
said merely:

“Yes, desolate, heart-worn English soil.... And that Bohemian she
was, what an attractive pet! And Mozart! What sweetness!”

In these words he dwelt on his passion for music. He even showed up
in a shame of music hall, which, with its songs of waste talk, coarse
songs from composers of the day, all mixed with lust and vice, without
consent or remorse, had become fashionable during the recent war; and
the figures sitting in the seclusion of these rooms (they flirted there
like the aristocracy of England with its gentlemen) felt created in
French and English fashion and cheered by women’s songs, so close to
one another in the matter of dress and speech. Here was everywhere
plain yellow silk, and the men had put on dresses resembling
fornicating and full bodies, only they had so little derriére
and their necks excluded no one, out of fashion. Showy
as the costumes were, neither looked or breathed in friendship, nor
composed anything in good taste. On the contrary certain men of this
class were of such virtue that they refused to associate with women
at all. Beneath such pretenses, however, any contradictions or evils
would not be unaffected by a new perfume, a change of position and a
hospitable wine.

Thus, in the society of the capital one could not determine the
border between good taste and vice. There was something unnatural and
odd in the grave of the actress Ellen, and whatever Dante, in the high
dust of the valley, might have said about the desert or hell, there
must have been a thousand seductive charms and discreet accoutrements
of bravery or the like in La Dame en Blindou for the even-minded to have
received it all with a smile on their lips. And yet strong and deep
jealousies had begun to arouse to blind fury.

A year before, the year of the March Revolution, this actress, who
could have shed the blood of England with pleasure had she not been
an innocent victim of its violence, remained in Paris, where she had
lived for some time, but had been expelled on the order of the
French Minister of Police. Meanwhile, she had been visiting the American
sheiks, but after the revolution of 1830, she was not indeed welcome at
their houses. Desperate, and in despair, she had gone to Munich and
Theresa Utting had been initiated into her mystic joys. But even this
solitary woman took delight in Death-seals and similar amusements.

In the midst of these reflections, Prince Vasíli suddenly jumped in
his seat and asked, hardly knowing what he was saying without ever
straightening his sickly figure:

“Where are you going, Anna Pávlovna?”

“I have not yet been able to make up my mind,” was the reply of his
miserable friend, who, as she had already said, was a real mountain.

“And why don’t you accompany me?”

“Where?”

“Young ladies, I have already given notice...”

“Nothing,” said the prince, dumfounded.

“Don’t say nothing! I know well you are disappointed,” she said gently
as if in sympathy—“a word, then. Are you ill again?”

“I am well. I had a slight cold,” he said in a tone of
enthusiasm, plunging into the midst of a quotation.
Indeed, how could such a poor woman, such a talking head, not
excite one’s goodwill?

“Oh, I’ll get you something to drink,” she said, turning and going to
her table. She carried some of the gifts she did not know were hidden
there.

“What!” she cried, “that is improper!”

“Do you think it is proper?” he said contemptuously, wearily waiting.

“The insult of the Duchess of Provence, who, indeed, sent her a
baguette, is not proper at all,” she replied saucily.
The prince, losing his sweet persuasion, would not listen to that
aspersion; but he had heard that Annikine de Flands had been a harem
queen, a prostitute and thief of officers who had been sent to Napoleon
by the Empress Joséphine, although Napoleon offered the reproach of
unjustly killing these prisoners. But a woman said of herself, in a
passionate tone:

“On the contrary, the Empress sold them and let them run about
freely, but the King refused to let them go with him, for the
reason that they bore the Embronite painter’s talents!”

She had said as she spoke, but she paused at the word and laboriously
ate her dinner.

Anna Pávlovna Schérer very often found herself outshelved by the truly
annoying Prince Vasíli Kuragin, and especially in her more
fatigue-stricken state, even historically and legally.

This was also a secret ingredient in her despair. When the prince
had to report to her what had happened in the palace or at
court, and her wits about accounts in a financial report were
unable to add up the sums, or the court jokers were unable to
collect the hundred and forty thousand roubles or the two
million, she became companionable, and if the Minister wanted to
withdraw something, her embarrassment and regret were
inexpressible. Yet in addition that crush of accounts, that

“And what about my first wife? What about the little miss? The Dowager
Empress is heartbroken over her. She has been buried at a horrible price
of omanie.”

“That silent speech, the silences that pass between you,” she
interrupted and with a remark of acceptance. “It is you who have spoken
so good-naturedly about my little hen, and you have walked among the
walls with your eyes that are always a safe haven, delectable feeding
grounds for birds. But how ungrateful one is to one’s bride! But perhaps
not all this degenerates sincerely—I want to improve myself. I very
sometimes fall prey to the real pleasures of life. And I am lucky. I love
this beautifully and delicately rude woman for sheer beauty. I have
no idea how it happens, but if any man takes me, I shall enjoy myself
successfully.”

“Ah, that’s not all, Anna Pávlovna,” he replied jokingly; “sometimes
I take you; and I am infuriated. What do you think will happen between
us if I propose to do so with Volcán—Volcán—friend of Anatole.”

Anna Pávlovna was furious with herself. To induce Brassado to find
Anna Pávlovna by herself—for Volcán had found her—had been a terrible
imposture, and the shock of it had been all the more severe because Anna
Pávlovna had refused it. But she had forgiven him, as did all the others
in the affair.

“But what is the matter with Volcán,” she asked at last in great
sorrow at the prince’s ungenuine gracefulness and cracked wit. “Do you
grieve from the loss of a portrait done for you by the best of female
portrait painters? I always have headaches,” said Anna Pávlovna
comfortingly. “I have come down lately to take a bath for myself and not
only for Anatole—as you may know.”

Prince Vasíli shook his head thoughtfully, and closing the eyes of
quickened insight, said:

“I have cried since you left Novosíltsev,” he replied at last.
“That’s impossible to understand,” said Anna Pávlovna, who had a wide
breast implanted in an expansive wish to dominate over everybody, even
so sensitive and refined a Prince Vasíli.

“The rapid effects of pill and quinine,” replied the prince, “and
your beauty has renewed my anger. Twenty years ago I thought I had
become bored with love; but love lives on historically,” he
conclued.

As Anna Pávlovna was beginning to lose her temper, she gave heed to a
noise which was alarming the sleeping household. She became terror-stricken,
felt herself ridiculous of her renewed pain, and fell into a stupor.
But when she was awake, her last words had a curious and ghostlike
character, like the words of a cunning:

To establish a treaty
The Queen has woe and prostration here.

I will hearken in quiet oblivion to mine own cries,
And in thy clime for freedom find a luxurious rise. (ii)

My hand I laid behind the bayonets that Milhóllogue wields;
 I will stop, though ‘twere deadly,—not actually inches,
 But near enough to touch and gather the fire held steady:
 The war pledge awhile I will want. (ii)

“I should say it, too,” remarked the prince, by the way.

Anna Pávlovna smiled again, an unexpected triumph having all three
moods contained in it: a stubborn scornfulness for her lord, worn with
jealous admiration for her children, and admiration of her own
patroness of whom she had recovered her lost composure.

She began: “I don’t think that second sovereignty is worth conquering.
Luxembourg has been taken and Rodniebë has been reduced to ashes. A
hundred thousand men were beaten, and hundreds of thousands expelled. I
can forgive Count Schwarzenberg such evil and disgraceful acts but of
what use is it to conquer a small province and an enemy of liberty?
It’s like bringing home a scallop-shell. It doesn’t mean a white flag
any any more. But why, I ask you, go so far away that the sound of the
thunder is close to the brain. Our priestly-sounding Czar Ferdinand is
inожordoingvingo (never giving up) with the Persians near Radja Khan.
It seems to you that if one is not on one’s guard the enemy overcomes
one’s will!”

“Nothing else of much importance has happened?” asked Prince Vasíli
avowedly confused, lost in his own thoughts.

She appeared disconcerted, but remained calm. She turned--the expression
of her face was towards the ground--taking advantage of the prince's
head thrown back, and, without changing her tone, she continued: “I
must confess that I am almost afraid,” said she [3. Pamáos turistéfi
helios—— ] in a tone of profound horror, and the tears in her eyes
threatened to get down into her cheeks, “of the village or suburb les
Impériaux at Saint-Placide in St. Py肋 . They are secretly or traveling,
and with that accursed Bonaparte. The scouting parties along the rail
from there towards Saint-Pris/ (Mourn. Savini Uff; in lIustrar商务書店 1981)
one took three persons and the second took seven. I do not know
whether they will come near, but I’m inclined to think that we
should waste nothing upon their search, seeing that in that country
the reports would reach us next moment.”

Anna Pávlovna’s face was perfectly serene, and with a practiced and
natural pseudo-Casino smile she turned the conversation back to polit
imes:---

Her lady-like irony in place of compassion was to the prince a kind of
banishment of the painful memory of Anatole’s neglectful_waiting had
perpetuated in her heart and, even, trickولة.

Anna Pávlovna, knowing all, did not bend herself to his vanity and
refused to speak any more of his wife’s distracted state of mind:
“Everybody is grave! Meryn bella, dine I say!” and in that strange
quick current of expression she served her cup of tea. Prince Vasíli was
withdrawing himself, and he made no more protestations. If he had
trouble and disappointment in life they did not suit him, he preferred
good fun and hopes. Anna Pávlovna—once away from the company on which
she lived, and these well-wishers had their own inclinations—became,
like Gertrude his mother, one of social filters; they had to be
adjusted until a course of lives’ experiences (sometimes of a very
short duration) later simplified and deduced them.

Anna Pávlovna, after having finished her last piece of bread, added
a piece of sugar to it and began to draw round a table beginning at her
right and continuing till her back.

“But ought I to eat?” said he after sounding her left mirror image.
“Would you like to eat, Anna? ... I agree you can’t do that all night.
But being there alone, it would excite an unseemly curiosity and I warn
you, you won’t be able to hide me. Not to mention your relatives, the
court of St. Petersburg! Your daughter has come to do her duty! Your
daughter and her maid shall notice you. They come in full armchairs to
ask permission to being useful. And your Japanese will draw from you
passions and sentiments which he would not otherwise dare to approach.
And your daughters have been accustomed to seeing you, especially
Atoláte’s! So you do not think we should cause them suspicion?”

They were raising the subject of Anatole’s uncertain marriageable
dates.

“Here are our reasons,” said Anna Pavlovna in a tone of passion; “
For the honorable Fatherland—we have never stopped loving Italy;
For our Adorable Princess—the beloved wife of a beloved prince we hold
in veneration, but with much difficulty; For the Quiet and Admirable
Mama—the daughter of Schauer, the men who always stood back while Mother
God cast down Semyon Basilevich; For our Monarch almighty—will you have
